Day 58 of 100 · Networking Deep Dive

Nginx Reverse Proxy

#100DaysOfCloudAndSecurityNetworking Deep DivePublished artifact recovered

A reverse proxy accepts client traffic and forwards it to application backends, moving routing, TLS and client-identity trust into an explicit infrastructure boundary.

Architecture / mental model

client → TLS/Nginx reverse proxy → loopback/private backend

How it works

Nginx can terminate TLS, route by hostname/path and forward requests to application processes that are not directly exposed to the internet.

Forwarded headers such as Host, X-Forwarded-Proto and X-Forwarded-For preserve context the backend may need, but the application must know which proxy sources are trusted before believing client-supplied forwarding headers.

Configuration should be validated before reload, then the full path inspected with both HTTP tools and logs rather than stopping at 'nginx -t succeeded.'

Hands-on reference

sudo nginx -t
sudo systemctl reload nginx
curl -I https://example.com
sudo tail -f /var/log/nginx/access.log
sudo ss -lntp

Verification

Send a request through the public hostname, correlate it in proxy and application logs, then confirm the backend is not unintentionally exposed on a public interface.

Field note / gotcha

Blindly trusting X-Forwarded-For lets a direct client claim an arbitrary source address. Trust only forwarding headers from known proxy networks/configuration.

Security considerations

Bind internal services to loopback/private interfaces where appropriate, protect proxy-to-backend traffic across untrusted networks and maintain explicit trusted-proxy configuration.

What I learned

A reverse proxy can strengthen architecture only when routing and trust boundaries are deliberate.
